title: Failover Orchestrator (RFO) — Design Draft (early)
linked_artifacts: slack:#architecture (thread: centralized trigger service vs distributed triggers)
content:
Context / why this doc exists
This is an early draft for the “Failover Orchestrator” service (working name: RFO). Goal is to get alignment between Platform (routing/control plane), SRE, and Infra on:
- What the orchestrator is responsible for vs. trigger engine vs. routing data plane
- The state machine we operate (incl. progressive failover)
- API ideas + audit surface (who did what, when, and why)
- Safety guardrails (don’t fail over into a worse place)
This is intentionally rough; the polished version should live in Confluence + an ADR.

Non-goals (for this doc)
- Not redesigning the routing stack or edge layer.
- Not defining every health signal/threshold (that’s trigger engine + signal contract).
- Not guaranteeing “zero customer impact” during real incidents.

Definitions (quick)
- Source region: region currently serving traffic for some slice.
- Target region: region we’d move traffic to.
- Slice: explicit scope of traffic (by route, model, customer tier, customer allowlist, etc.).
- Progressive failover: shift traffic in steps (e.g., 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%) with verification gates.
- Mode:
  - monitor-only: compute decisions but do not execute changes
  - manual-approve: system proposes, human approves execution
  - auto: system executes if all safety conditions pass

High-level architecture sketch
Inputs:
- Region health signals (aggregated): error rate, p95/p99 latency, streaming disconnect rate, dependency health, saturation/headroom, synthetic probes.
- Config/policy: thresholds, hysteresis, windows, “safe-to-failover” checks, progressive steps.
- Operator intents: enable/disable, override, scope limiting (only low-risk routes), etc.

Core responsibilities of RFO
1) State machine + orchestration
- Owns state transitions (proposed → executing → completed / aborted).
- Executes routing changes through existing primitives (internal policy store and/or edge/DNS).
- Enforces hold-down timers and prevents flappy transitions.

2) Safety guard enforcement (independent verification)
- Before moving traffic, verify target region capacity headroom + dependency health.
- Sanity-check routing policy updates (no invalid targets, no loops, TTL constraints, etc.).

3) Audit + observability
- Emit durable audit events for each decision + action.
- Expose current state (per region, per slice), last transitions, and why.

What RFO is NOT
- It should not be the system deciding “is region unhealthy?” — that comes from Trigger Engine output.
- It should not be the authoritative source of capacity metrics — it consumes capacity signals from Fleet/Capacity Ops systems.

Service boundaries (proposed)
A) Health Signal Aggregator
- Normalizes raw metrics/probes → region_health{region, signal, value, window, confidence}
- Stores recent history for evaluation/audit and “what did we see?” debugging.

B) Trigger Evaluation Engine
- Reads region_health signals + config
- Outputs: trigger verdicts and recommended actions, e.g.
  - trigger.fire(region=us-east-1, severity=failover_recommended, scope=hosted/chat)
  - or: trigger.fire(... severity=degrade_only)
- This engine should also output “explain” payload (which signals contributed) for audit.

C) Failover Orchestrator (this doc)
- Consumes trigger verdicts + operator mode
- Runs state machine; executes changes via Routing Policy Store + Edge/DNS hooks

D) Routing Policy Store + Data Plane
- Applies policy to route requests. (We should keep this as dumb as possible—policy in, behavior out.)

State machine (draft)
We likely need a per-(slice, source_region) state machine.

States (names TBD; current suggestion)
- HEALTHY: no active mitigation; serving normally.
- DEGRADED_LOCAL_MITIGATION: we are in “degraded but available” mode; load shedding/timeouts/fallbacks may be applied locally.
- FAILOVER_PROPOSED: trigger recommends failover; waiting for approval (if in manual-approve) or safety checks.
- FAILOVER_EXECUTING: actively moving traffic (progressive steps).
- FAILED_OVER: traffic primarily served by target region; source region is drained or minimal traffic.
- RECOVERY_PROPOSED: source region appears healthy again; considering rollback/restore.
- RECOVERY_EXECUTING: progressively restoring traffic to source region.
- ABORTED: attempt aborted due to stop conditions (safety check failed or operator abort).

Events
- trigger.degrade: request to enter degraded mitigation
- trigger.failover: request to fail over
- operator.approve_failover / operator.abort / operator.override_target
- safety_checks.passed / safety_checks.failed
- step.completed / step.failed
- hold_down.expired

Transitions (very rough)
HEALTHY
  -> (trigger.degrade) DEGRADED_LOCAL_MITIGATION
  -> (trigger.failover) FAILOVER_PROPOSED

DEGRADED_LOCAL_MITIGATION
  -> (trigger.failover) FAILOVER_PROPOSED
  -> (signals recover AND hold-down expired) HEALTHY

FAILOVER_PROPOSED
  -> (mode=auto AND safety_checks.passed) FAILOVER_EXECUTING
  -> (mode=manual-approve AND operator.approve AND safety_checks.passed) FAILOVER_EXECUTING
  -> (safety_checks.failed OR operator.abort) ABORTED

FAILOVER_EXECUTING
  -> (all steps completed) FAILED_OVER
  -> (stop condition hit OR operator.abort) ABORTED (with best-effort rollback to last known good)

FAILED_OVER
  -> (trigger says target also unhealthy) ??? (this is the ugly case; see risks)
  -> (source appears healthy AND hold-down expired) RECOVERY_PROPOSED

RECOVERY_PROPOSED
  -> (mode=auto AND safety_checks.passed) RECOVERY_EXECUTING
  -> (manual-approve AND operator.approve AND safety_checks.passed) RECOVERY_EXECUTING
  -> (operator.abort) FAILED_OVER

RECOVERY_EXECUTING
  -> (restore steps completed) HEALTHY
  -> (stop condition) FAILED_OVER (stay failed over)

Important: hold-down + hysteresis
- We must not bounce between regions.
- Minimum time in FAILED_OVER before attempting recovery.
- Minimum time in HEALTHY before allowing failover again for same slice.
- Trigger engine already has hysteresis, but orchestrator should still implement hold-down timers as a last line.

Progressive failover mechanics (draft)
We need a generic mechanism to “shift X% of slice to target region” while preserving rollback ability.

Config shape idea (not final)
- slice_id: hosted/chat-default
- source_region: us-east-1
- candidate_targets: [us-west-2, eu-west-1]
- steps: [1, 5, 25, 50, 100]
- step_verification_window_sec: 180
- step_success_criteria:
  - error_rate_delta <= +0.2%
  - p99 <= 2.5s
  - streaming_disconnect_rate <= threshold
- stop_conditions:
  - p99 > hard_limit OR 5xx > hard_limit for 2m
  - target_capacity_headroom < min_headroom
  - dependency health red

Rollback model
- Keep “previous policy version” pointer for each step.
- If step fails verification, rollback to prior policy version and enter ABORTED (or remain in DEGRADED_LOCAL_MITIGATION if that was active).

Open question: can we do progressive failover purely in internal routing policy store (preferred) vs requiring DNS/edge? DNS TTL makes progressiveness coarse unless we have per-request routing in edge.

Interfaces / APIs (early)
Audience:
- Control plane services, SRE tooling, incident bot
- Possibly Console (read-only) later

We need both a control API and a read-only status/audit API.

Read-only APIs (must have)
GET /v1/failover/slices
- returns list of slices with current state + active target

GET /v1/failover/slices/{slice_id}/status
- state, source, target, current_step, last_transition_at
- trigger summary: verdict, top contributing signals
- safety checks last evaluated + results

GET /v1/failover/slices/{slice_id}/audit?since=...
- append-only event feed

Control APIs (gated by RBAC; likely only oncall + specific groups)
POST /v1/failover/slices/{slice_id}:propose
- allows operator to create a proposal (rare; mostly triggers should propose)

POST /v1/failover/slices/{slice_id}:approve
- approve a proposal in manual-approve mode

POST /v1/failover/slices/{slice_id}:abort
- abort in-progress

POST /v1/failover/slices/{slice_id}:override
- body: { target_region?, step_override?, mode_override?, reason }

POST /v1/failover/global:mode
- set global mode: monitor-only, manual-approve, auto
- should require change management (release gating) + audit

Security/RBAC notes
- Need a dedicated RBAC group (e.g., rfo-operators) with break-glass for IC.
- Audit logs must include actor identity, request id, and linked incident (if available).

Events / pubsub
RFO should emit events for:
- state transitions
- step transitions
- stop condition triggers
- safety check failures
This feeds:
- incident-bot postings in #incidents
- dashboards
- longer-term audit retention

Dependency integration (draft)
Routing policy store integration
- Assume we can write a policy “weight” per target region for a slice.
- We need versioning and atomic updates.
- Must support “read current policy” to compute diffs and rollback.

Edge/DNS integration
- Only for cases where data plane routing cannot override region selection.
- Prefer to keep DNS changes as last resort (slow + caching).
- If we must use DNS:
  - TTL strategy must be explicit
  - Progressive steps may be limited (e.g., cannot reliably do 1%)

Capacity / headroom integration
- Inputs (authoritative?): GPU pool headroom, queue depth, admission control saturation.
- Query API (preferred) vs reading metrics directly.
- Safety check logic should be simple and explicit: “min headroom = N GPUs or X% capacity + queue depth < threshold”.

Dependency health checks
- Needed deps: model artifact store, auth, billing/rate-limit, tokenization, logging pipeline, etc.
- Must differentiate “regional impairment” vs “global dependency issue” (don’t fail over if dependency is global).

Safe-to-failover checks (must have before auto mode)
1) Target region has sufficient capacity headroom
- For the specific slice. Worst case: check aggregate headroom + conservative multiplier.

2) Target region is healthy by the same health signal contract
- If target is already degraded, do not pile on.

3) Routing policy sanity
- Validate new policy doesn’t violate constraints (allowed regions, customer data residency constraints, dedicated isolation constraints).

4) Blast radius limit
- Never fail over “everything” at once in early rollout.
- Configurable max traffic shift per time window.

Degraded-but-available vs failover
We should have a first-class “degraded mitigation” path that is NOT failover:
- shed low-priority traffic (free tier / best-effort)
- tighten timeouts
- switch to fallback model variants (if configured)
- disable expensive features (tool calling?) for impacted slice (maybe too product-y; parking lot)

Key design question: should RFO own degraded mitigations, or should a separate “degradation controller” do that? My leaning: RFO owns “traffic moves” and a separate component owns local mitigations. But we may start with both as part of orchestrator to keep fewer moving parts.

Failure modes / risks (brain dump)
- Flappy triggers cause oscillation
  Mitigation: hysteresis in trigger engine + hold-down in orchestrator + manual override always available.

- False positive health signals (synthetics, network probes) cause unnecessary failover
  Mitigation: signal confidence scoring; require multiple independent signals; progressive canary step with strict stop conditions.

- Failing over into insufficient capacity → worse outage
  Mitigation: conservative capacity checks; failover only a subset first; build capacity buffers per region.

- DNS propagation/TTL makes incident response slower + harder to reason about
  Mitigation: prefer internal routing policy; if DNS is required, pre-plan TTL strategy and define what “complete” means.

- Split-brain / conflicting controllers
  Mitigation: single writer principle; RFO is the only actor allowed to write failover-related policy keys (enforced via IAM/RBAC).

- Data residency / private deployment constraints
  Mitigation: per-slice allowlist of legal targets. RFO must reject invalid targets even if trigger recommends.

- Target dependency is global-down (billing/auth) so failover doesn’t help
  Mitigation: dependency gating checks; require regional scope evidence.

- “Double failover” scenario (source impaired, fail to target, then target impaired)
  Mitigation: explicit policy: do not chain automatically; require manual IC decision + smaller canary steps; consider a third region only if pre-approved.

Alternatives considered (very early)
1) Distributed per-service triggers + local actions
Pros: fewer central components.
Cons: inconsistent behavior, hard audit trail, hard to coordinate progressive failover, each team rebuilds safety logic.

2) Keep manual runbook only
Pros: simplest.
Cons: slow MTTR, operator errors, inconsistent decision-making, hard to test.

3) Edge-level anycast/BGP failover
Pros: potentially fast and transparent.
Cons: operational complexity; not aligned with current architecture; harder to do per-slice/tier failover.

4) External managed traffic manager
Pros: faster to adopt?
Cons: doesn’t understand our internal capacity/model constraints; hard to integrate with routing policies and customer tiers.

Open questions / TODOs
- Scope model for “slice”: what is the minimal unit we can safely shift? (route+model+tier?)
- Dedicated: do we allow orchestrator to touch Dedicated routing automatically, or start with Hosted only?
- How do we represent customer-specific constraints (e.g., pinned region, private endpoints, compliance) in policy validation?
- What is our single source of truth for “current routing weights”? (must be readable + versioned)
- Where do we store audit events? (DB table + append-only log?) and retention requirements.
- Interaction with release gating: who can flip from monitor-only → manual-approve → auto, and what’s the checklist?
- Do we need an explicit “maintenance window / planned test” flag to adjust alerting + comms?

Next steps (proposed)
- Align on service boundaries + state machine names with SRE (Miles, Tomáš) + Smart Routing (Mina).
- Draft config schema for slices + progressive steps.
- Define minimal APIs for v0 (status + approve/abort/override).
- List required dependencies and confirm owners (capacity signals, routing policy store write path, edge/DNS hooks).
- Convert this into Confluence service page + ADR (see adr-0247 linkage).

Notes to self
- Keep the v0 boring: monitor-only first, then manual-approve for one low-risk slice, then auto after multiple game days.
- If we can avoid DNS for Hosted, do it. DNS will burn time during incidents and make verification ambiguous.
- Invest early in audit “why did we do this?” because every enterprise escalation will ask for it.
